Dandu Malikarjuna ...Petitioner/Accused  Petitioner/Accused  AND The State Of Andhra Pradesh and ...Respondent/Complainant(S)
 Respondent/Complainant(S)

The Court made the following:
ORDER:

The present Criminal petition is filed to call for the records pertaining to C.C. No.423 of 2018 in Crime No.246 of 2018 of Mydukur (u/g) Police Station, and the police have laid the charge sheet for the offence under Sections 406, 420 IPC and to quash the same.

2. The brief facts of the case are that LW1 intended to purchase an extent of land Ac.7.76 cents in Survey No.1384/1B and 1394 of Settivaripalli Village of Mydukur Mandal @ Rs.13,50,000/- per acre and accordingly paid an amount of Rs.25,00,000/- towards advance, thereby the petitioner as well as the respondent-complainant executed an agreement of sale to that effect on 23.12.2010 with Dandu Malikarjuna vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/136456369/
1 conditions.

sentences.text: Later, the 2nd respondent-defacto-complainant came to know that the land is not Patta land and that is D.K.T. Patta land and thereby he demanded the petitioner/accused for payment of the amount and the petitioner/accused has paid part amount.
Therefore, he lodged a report to the police to take appropriate action against the petitioner for cheating him to sell the land where he has no title over the property.

3. Now the said complaint was assailed in the present Criminal Petition on the ground that it is a civil dispute arising out of contract when there is breach of contract the remedy is to file Civil Suit for the enforcement of contract and if at all

the 2nd respondent/complainant is aggrieved he has to file a civil suit for recovery of the amount and also contends that the complaint filed by the 2nd respondent is not maintainable as the respondent/complainant has not followed the guidelines `framed by the Hon'ble Apex Court in Priyanka Srivastava and another v. State of Uttar Pradesh 1.

entities.text: Priyanka Srivastava and another v. State of Uttar Pradesh
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
4. Heard Sri Lovaneet Kumar Sharma, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner and Sri V.
Nitesh, learned Public Prosecutor.
5.

It is the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner herein that to pressurize the accused and to bring them to their own terms or to enforce obligation arising out of breach of contract at which commercial transactions instead of approaching civil court with a view to realize money at the earliest has filed the present complaint and in order to give cloak of criminal offence, the present complaint was lodged and mere breach of contract would not attract the ingredients of Section 420 IPC and the respondent/ 1 (2015) 6 SCC 287 complainant has to file a civil suit as held by the Hon'ble Apex Court in catena of decisions, and also contended that the complaint itself is not maintainable in view of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Priyanka Srivastava case (supra 1).
6.

Per contra, fulminating the contentions raised by the petitioner, the counsel appearing for the 2nd respondent/defacto complainant would submit that the petitioner has entered into an agreement with the respondent/complainant for the land where the petitioner/accused has no right or title over the property and it is a DKT patta land.
Therefore, the contention raised by the petitioner that a Civil Suit is only maintainable is not acceptable as there is a dishonest intention on the part of the petitioner/accused.
Therefore, he would urge to dismiss the quash petition and it is a case for trial whether the petitioner has any dishonest intention or not has to arrive from the evidence.

7. In G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P.2, the Hon'ble Apex Court held that while exercising jurisdiction under section 482 of the Code has to be exercised with a great care and not to examine the matter superficially.

entities.text: G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P.2
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is to be seen if a matter, which is essentially of civil nature, has been given a cloak of criminal offence.
Criminal proceedings are not a short cut of other remedies available in law.
Before issuing process, a criminal Court has to exercise a great deal of caution.
For the accused it is a serious matter.

8. In case of S.W. Palanitkar and others -Vrs.- State of Bihar3, it is held as follows:-
Dandu Malikarjuna vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/136456369/

sentences.text: Many a times, complaints are filed under section 200 Cr.P.C. by the parties with an oblique motive or for collateral purposes to harass, to wreak vengeance to pressurize the accused to bring them to their own terms or to enforce the obligations arising out of breach of contract touching commercial transactions instead of approaching civil courts with a view to realize money at the earliest.

It is also to be kept in mind that when parties commit a wrongful act constituting a criminal offence satisfying necessary ingredients of an offence, they cannot be allowed to walk away with an 2 (2000) 2 SCC 636 3 (2002) 1 SCC 241 impression that no action could be taken against them on criminal side.
A wrongful or illegal act such as criminal breach of trust, misappropriation, cheating or defamation may give rise to action both on civil as well as on criminal side.

When it is clear from the complaint and sworn statements that necessary ingredients of constituting an offence are made out, may be parties are entitled to proceed on civil side only in a given situation in the absence of an act constituting an offence but not to proceed against the accused in a criminal prosecution.

Hence before issuing a process, a Magistrate has to essentially keep in mind the scheme contained in the provisions of sections 200-203 of Cr.P.C. keeping in mind the position of law stated above and pass an order judiciously and not mechanically or in routine manner."
9.

The crux that it postulate is the intention of the person who induces the victim of his representation and not the nature of the transaction which would become decisive in discerning whether there was commission of offence or not.

10. In Hridaya Ranjan Pd. Verma (V) State of Bihar4, it is held as follows:
"15. On a reading of the section it is manifest that in the definition there are set forth two separate classes of 4 2000 (4) SCC 168 acts which the person deceived may be induced to do.

entities.text: Hridaya Ranjan Pd. Verma (V) State of Bihar4
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the first place he may be induced fraudulently or dishonestly to deliver any property to any person.
The second class of acts set forth in the section is the doing or omitting to do anything which the person deceived would not do or omit to do if he were not so deceived.
In the first class of cases, the inducing must be fraudulent or dishonest.
In the second class of acts, the inducing must be intentional but not fraudulent or dishonest.
11. Counsel appearing for respondent would submit that it is falsely represented that unofficial respondent/defacto- complainant had clear title over the property in question.

The learned counsel for the unofficial respondent/defacto complainant would submit that the accused induced the complainant to part with a sum of Rs.25,00,000/- and therefore committed an offence of cheating under Section 420 of the IPC and latter the accused has repaid an amount of Rs 19, 15, 000/-
12.

In Kamal Shivaji Pokarnekar v. State of Maharashtra5, the Hon'ble Apex Court held that concealment of title over the property while making the representations to 5 (2019) 14 SCC 350 the complainant regarding clear title of the subject property is a deception under section 415 IPC.

sentences.text:
petitioner accused has concealed the fact that the subject property is DKT Patta, and therefore, as per provision of Section 415 of the Indian Penal Code, a dishonest concealment of facts is a deception.
13.

The contention raised by learned counsel for the petitioner is not acceptable as rightly contested by learned counsel for the respondents/defacto complainant the petitioner has tried to alienate the property where he is not having any right, title over the property and the land is admittedly DKT patta land.
Hence, the contentions raised by the petitioner is that the present complaint is filed to give a cloak of criminal offence, is rejected.

14. The other contentions raised by the 2nd contention raised by the counsel appearing for the petitioner is that the complaint is not maintainable in view of the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court referred supra (1).
15.
It is Court that has forwarded a complaint to the police under Section 200 Cr.P.C.

Even assuming that the petitioner herein has prayed to refer the matter to the police under Section 156 (3)
of Cr.P.C. that cannot be pressed into service as the police has already investigated the case and filed charge sheet and the order referring to the police has been merged in the chargesheet.

16. Viewing in any manner, the contention raised by the counsel appearing for the petitioner that the complaint is not maintainable for not following the guidelines enumerated in Priyanka Srivastava case is unsustainable for the reasons mentioned above.

17. The Kamal Shivaji Pokarnekar (supra 5) case is squarely applies to the present case, wherein it is observed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that criminal complaints cannot be quashed only on the ground that the allegations made therein appear to be of a civil nature, and if the ingredients of the offence alleged against are prima facie made out in the complaint, the criminal proceedings shall not be interdicted, against the accused, would decide the said complaint on its own merits and in accordance with law, uninfluenced by the observations if any made herein above.
All contentions raised on merits are kept open for being agitated before the Trial Court.

The question as to whether the Petitioners accused committed breach of trust and/or cheated the complainant would be decided only during trial after giving opportunity to the parties to lead evidence in that regard.
18. Accordingly, the Criminal Petition is dismissed.
As a sequel, miscellaneous petitions, if any, pending in this criminal petition shall stand closed.
